How to Play

Tam Cúc (Three Chrysanthemums) is a traditional multi-trick card game with an asymmetrical deck based on Chinese chess (Cờ Tướng). Goal: collect the most cards by winning tricks.

RankNameTranslationQty / colour
1 (highest)TướngGeneral1
2SĩAdvisor2
3TượngElephant2
4XeChariot2
5PháoCannon2
6MãHorse2
7 (lowest)TốtSoldier5

Valid combinations (one colour only; Red beats Black of the same type and rank)

  • Single: any card.
  • Pair: two identical cards.
  • Three-card combo: Tướng-Sĩ-Tượng or Xe-Pháo-Mã (no bridging).
  • Four / Five Sons: 4–5 Soldiers of one colour.

Steps

  1. House: deal face-up calling ranks; whoever gets the card just called leads first.
  2. Deal the whole deck evenly (4 players → 8 each).
  3. Instant win: Four/Five Sons shown before play wins the round.
  4. Call the trick: the House puts 1–3 cards face-down and announces it.
  5. Follow: clockwise, everyone plays the same number of cards face-down (or sacrifices unmatched cards).
  6. Reveal: the highest valid combo wins all the cards and leads next. If you will lose, you may secretly concede and keep your cards hidden.

Play until all cards are gone: most cards wins. (In the game here you duel one hero: 8 cards each, as in the 4-player deal, and the other 16 cards sit out.)

How it is preserved and received today

Tam Cúc has moved from everyday pastime to nostalgic cultural relic.

The full deck: every rank in Red and Black.

A Lunar New Year tradition. Families gather by the fire on winter nights, waiting for bánh chưng to cook; the long cards mean reunion and festive warmth, especially in the North.

Eclipsed by modern games. Tiến Lên, Tá Lả (Phỏm) and Xì Dách, played with the 52-card Western deck, now dominate cafés and friend groups.

Romanticised in literature. Hoàng Cầm's poem "Cây Tam Cúc" uses the red and black generals to evoke youth, spring and subtle romance.

Digital preservation. Mobile apps and web portals let a new generation learn the rules and play against AI without hunting for a physical deck.

South · Nghệ thuật thắt lá dừa

Giữa Sài Gòn có ông lão bán cào cào bằng lá dừa, gìn giữ tuổi thơ

In the rush of modern Saigon, commuters suddenly spot their childhood: grasshoppers, fish, crabs and herons woven from young nipa-palm leaves, swaying from a street corner.
Lê Minh, 66, was once a painter with his own gallery. As his eyesight faded he put down the brush and returned to his first love: shaping palm leaves, learned as a boy from a street master.
With nimble hands he now weaves 21 different animals. He sits at ever-changing crossroads, so regulars often struggle to find him. Foreign visitors buy them too, calling them the true beauty of Vietnamese folk art.
His children could support him, yet he will not stop: “Tuổi thơ mà, ai lại đi định giá.” He wants kids to look up from screens and learn how their grandparents played. Now it's your turn: scroll on and weave.

Cách thắt con cào cào

Chuẩn bị nguyên liệu

  • 1 nhánh lá dừa nước non (hoặc lá dừa thường màu vàng nhạt, độ dai tốt) dài khoảng 30-40cm.
  • Kéo hoặc dao rọc.
Chuẩn bị: lá dừa, kéo và đôi tay khéo léo.
